BHP said: "Our focus remains on making constructive progress towards fair and reasonable agreements."

"We are committed to continuing to bargain in good faith on new workplace agreements across our iron ore operations and believe that the involvement of the independent Fair Work Commission is the most constructive way to achieve the best outcome," the miner said.

The ETU was hoping the strike would pressure a shift from BHP.

"We anticipated that BHP might revise their position and not continue down the tone-deaf path that they have so far in bargaining," Mr Woodage said.

Workers were met by "Scabby the Cat" during the strike. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

"BHP should be able to clearly understand our claims. They're not difficult."

After the FWC bargaining meetings, the ETU will go back to its members for instructions on what to do next.

Mr Woodage said that could mean further negotiations through the FWC, direct talks with BHP or "they might instruct us they wish to participate in more strike action".

What are the broader implications?

Alexis Vassiley, a lecturer in work and employment relations at Edith Cowan University, said there had not been a strike at BHP since 2000, with what the CME calls "a model of direct collaboration between workers and the companies" largely the norm.

Dr Vassiley said this strike had broken that mould.

Alexis Vassiley says this strike has broken that mould. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

"It broke the drought of industrial action in the Pilbara. The last time it happened anywhere in the iron ore industry was Rio Tinto train drivers in 2008," he said.

"For decades and decades and decades, not only have workers not been taking industrial action, but there also hasn't been union influence over pay and conditions.

" So if there were to be a successful enterprise agreement negotiated at BHP ports, that would be the first time that has happened outside of train drivers in decades and perhaps could set a precedent. "

Dr Vassiley said power dynamics could change.

200 workers walked off the job for the eight-hour strike. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

"It's not one individual negotiating up against a multinational corporation; rather, it's a group of workers negotiating collectively," he said.

"There's a very long way to go, but one outcome could be that there becomes more of a collective voice for workers and more of a say at work for workers at BHP ports."

Scaremongering denial

Dr Vassiley predicted a potentially long union campaign involving more industrial action.

"It seems that is the way workers can pressure the company," he said.

The CMEWA's Aaron Morey claimed that could impact workers' wages.

Aaron Morey says there was a lack of productivity. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

He also denied he had been scaremongering on the financial impact of the strike and maintained international investors were watching.

BHP workers to strike as company reaches record production As hundreds of BHP workers prepare to down tools in a landmark strike, BHP's latest report reveals its highest ever production of iron ore.

"Irrespective of the number of people who got involved, you cannot deny that this has an impact on productivity," he said.

"And nothing is more important when it comes to wages.

"If we continue to challenge productivity in this way, it's going to be harder and harder to achieve the wage increases that workers deserve."

Mr Woodage, from the ETU, tried to hose down suggestions strikes could now break out across the Pilbara in other mining companies.

"No, because the ability to take action is a rigorous process through the Fair Work Act and we're not at that process with any other miner in the Pilbara," he said.

World.title: Smelter clean-up bill likely to be funded by Tasmanian taxpayers, experts say
World.content:
Responsibility for rehabilitating and cleaning up the Liberty Bell Bay site could ultimately fall to the Tasmanian government, according to legal experts, after administrators failed to secure a buyer for the embattled manganese smelter.

Administrators announced on Thursday that they had been unable to secure a buyer for the northern Tasmanian smelter, triggering its immediate closure and leaving about 200 workers without jobs, while also raising questions about the future of the industrial site.

'Substantial clean-up' needed for smelter Australia's only manganese alloy smelter has closed, leaving the future of the site uncertain and the country more reliant on imported alloys for steel production.

While the Tasmanian government has not ruled out another operator taking over the site, it is likely to become a major financial burden if it is closed down.

"This particular site will need a significant rehabilitation if it does come to that kind of full closure," Tasmanian Minister for Business, Industry and Resources Felix Ellis said.

"Now obviously that'll be something that the owners will need to work through, and the government is monitoring that situation closely."

Workers at the Liberty Bell Bay smelter have been hoping for a new buyer. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

In October, a report by William Buck, the administrator of Sanjeev Gupta's Whyalla Ports, estimated the rehabilitation costs of Liberty Bell Bay to be about $200 million if the facility was closed.

Asked on Friday whether that figure was accurate, Mr Ellis said it was "around that mark".

"It depends, of course, on the scale of rehabilitation, but I can definitely indicate it is substantial," he said.

So, if that is the case, who pays for it?

The operation at Liberty Bell Bay is Australia's only manganese smelter. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Tasmanian taxpayers likely left with bill

At it currently stands, the administrators are responsible for the site and the associated clean-up and remediation costs.

However, according to University of Sydney professor Jason Harris, an expert in corporate and insolvency law, that is likely to change if the company enters liquidation.

The smelter was established in the 1960s and has had several owners. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

"Liquidators have a power that administrators don't," he said.

"If the company goes into liquidation, what would happen is the liquidators would be able to disclaim the property.

" Then the land will go back to the state government, as the kind of ultimate owner for the land that no-one owns. They'd be responsible for the land. "

Jason Harris says if "no-one wants to buy it … it will become the state government's problem". (ABC News: Laurence Curson)

On Friday, Mr Ellis did not directly answer whether the state government would undertake and pay for the site's rehabilitation if the company was unable to.

"It's too early. This is still a hypothetical at this stage," he said.

"The owners currently have an obligation around the clean-up and to ensure the site is rehabilitated if the business goes into full closure

Professor Harris said a full closure would be an "extreme outcome" and he suspected the government would work with administrators to find an alternative.

"The EPA and the state government do not want to have a $200 million bill lobbed on their front door," he said.

"So they would want to be working with the administrators to try and sell the asset if they can, or facilitate the sale of the asset if they can, even if it means that they need to put in more financial support."

" Maybe no-one wants to buy it, in which case it will become the state government's problem. "

When asked why a clean-up fund was not a condition of ownership of the smelter, Felix Ellis said that was a "question for people in generations past". (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Professor Harris said another option available to liquidators was to sue former directors, if there were legal grounds to do so.

Adelaide University emeritus professor Christopher Symes, an expert in insolvency law, said under corporations law, there was no priority given to environmental claims in a liquidation process.

"If the liquidator goes down the path of disclaiming … the land that the smelter is based upon, and there are clean-up costs there, assuming that there's very little in the company, then there's no way that the liquidator has to spend what's very little left on clean-up. There may be other things to pay, maybe even ahead of clean-up."

He said if, after selling off assets and paying other creditors, there was a balance left over, then EPA clean-up notices could be dealt with.

But he said the liquidators had to comply with the Corporations Act, and the EPA would ultimately be treated as unsecured creditors.

"And as we sort of know, unsecured creditors in liquidation, in any company that's in liquidation, pretty much get nothing. The money's run out before they become liquidated," he said.

The smelter was a major employer in the region. (Supplied)

What's next?

Tasmanian Minerals, Manufacturing and Energy Council (TMEC) chief executive Ray Mostogl said the site could be mothballed, as was often the case with mining sites.

"Arguably, the same logic applies to something like this, but the infrastructure on this site is considerably different to the infrastructure on a mine site," he said.

" The longer it sits idle, the longer it sits cold … more and more damage occurs, and the more the materials deteriorate, so it becomes a much bigger cost burden to restart it than it is today. "

"I imagine that mothballing it would not be a long-term [solution]. It might be an interim position until there is a better way to do some rehabilitation."

Ray Mostogl says while some parts of the site could be sold off, other aspects, such as soil contamination, are harder to fix. (ABC News)

The administrators have said that in the short term they will keep on a small number of workers to safely demobilise the site, realise the sale of assets, and meet environmental and regulatory obligations.

In addition to assets such as vehicles and equipment, Mr Mostogl said parts of the land, such as the electric substation, offices, and workshops, could be sold and used by other businesses.

But he said the industrial plant itself would be less straightforward to rehabilitate.

"The reality is, I think you'd have to demolish the industrial part of the plant, the actual facilities, and it would just be cut up for steel basically, he said.

"It would be basically dropped to the ground. You'd cut the whole thing up and then there'd be a cost of remediating the soil."

The smelter was bought by Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance in 2020 following a period of uncertainty under its previous owner, South32. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

No clean-up fund in place

Mr Ellis said, unlike mining operations, Liberty Bell Bay was not required to pay the money into a government fund to be used in the event of a permanent shutdown to pay for rehabilitation and the environmental clean-up.

"There's funds for mining, but this particular site doesn't have the same kind of protections. It is an older, historic site," he said.

When asked why a similar requirement had not been imposed on Liberty Bell Bay, he said it was a "question for people in generations past".

A spokesperson for the Environment Protection Authority said Liberty Bell Bay was currently subject to an environmental protection order that included decommissioning and rehabilitation requirements.

"The EPA is participating in a coordinated approach by the government to understand options for the site, including management of environmental liabilities," they said.

Union says deal failed due to power concessions

On Friday, unions said the cost of electricity from state-owned Hydro Tasmania was central to the sale of the smelter falling through.

The state government said the consortium had requested a two-year deferral of electricity and transmission charges … as well as tens of millions of dollars in subsidies on top of already discounted power.

It said $155 million of support had been put on the table over the past decade.

The unions are urging all parties to resume sale negotiations.

World.title: 'Filthy, polluted': Trump's Canada threat as World Cup smoke risk looms
World.content:
Spanish star Mikel Merino can smell and see the smoke from the Canadian wildfires that are making for hazy conditions across large parts of the US.

But Merino is trying not to focus on it.

It remains unclear how much, if at all, the smoke will affect the World Cup final on Monday morning AEST. The World Health Organization forecast calls for an improvement to "moderate" air quality in New Jersey.

Spain's Mikel Merino trains outside in a session that experts said should have taken place indoors. (Getty Images: Pablo Garcia/Soccrates)

"For a game that is as important as a World Cup final, you have to be able to shut out external factors as much as possible," Merino said.

"Luckily, we are being careful with every detail thanks to the federation and the organisers of the World Cup."

Spain practised outside in hazardous conditions in East Hanover, New Jersey, on Thursday, alarming experts who thought the team should have held the session inside instead. Messages sent to FIFA and the Spanish Football Association asking whether that was considered or possible were not returned.

Spain trains in 'hazardous' air as wildfire smoke drifts from Canada World Cup finalists Spain train in "hazardous" conditions in New Jersey as wildfires cause excessive smoke in the north-east of the United States.

Air quality improved Friday, but uncertainty lies in what will follow, with up to 3 centimetres of rain expected to fall Saturday.

"Following that, it looks like there is another smoky air mass following in behind that system, but it's not clear right now how much or how it might reach New York or New Jersey when it comes to [the final]," said Mark Parrington, senior scientist at the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.

"If the fire intensity really picks up again … it's possible it puts more smoke into the atmosphere that then might quickly follow that rain event."

Jonathan Belles, senior meteorologist for The Weather Channel app and weather.com, expects to have improved confidence in the forecast as game time gets closer.

"The question is whether smoke behind that [rain] system reaches ground level over northern New Jersey on Sunday and, if so, how concentrated it becomes," Mr Belles said.

"Current forecast models range from little to no ground-level smoke to levels that could become more concerning for players and fans."

Smoke from wildfires, which are burning more and more of North America, attacks nearly every system in the body, killing tens of thousands of people a year, numerous medical studies show.

It attacks the body immediately, spiking asthma cases, with increased ambulance runs within hours.

Smoke can trigger inflammation in different parts of the body, often attacking a person's weakest points, which can then cascade into different effects of an immune system trying to fight a nasty irritant, doctors and scientists say.

There could be an impact on players's performance even if the air conditions are moderate, according to the University of California San Diego's professor of medicine, Chantal Darquenne.

"It's kind of a dose-dependent effect," Professor Darquenne said.

"If it's moderate, it's going to be less of an effect but it's still going to be there, especially because they are doing vigorous exercise during these events."

Trump threatens Canada with tariffs

US President Donald Trump was set to meet with FIFA President Gianni Infantino ahead of the final.

Members of the administration, including Andrew Giuliani, the executive director of the White House FIFA Task Force, have been discussing the matter with football's governing body and monitoring the wildfire situation, according to a White House official.

US President Donald Trump leaves Washington DC for New York in Marine One amid smoky conditions. (Getty Images: Tom Brenner)

The person was granted anonymity to confirm internal discussions.

Mr Trump said he would impose new tariffs on Canada over the wildfire smoke but made no mention of the World Cup final.

"We are holding Canada responsible," the US president posted on his social media site.

He added that, "[The US] is being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air, the quality of which is dangerous and totally unacceptable!"

Roughly 80,000 fans are expected at the final, which takes place in the large, open-air stadium in the Meadowlands, which is home to the NFL's New York Giants and Jets.

A fan wears a mask during an air-quality warning prior to a baseball game between the New York Mets and the Philadelphia Phillies. (AP: Chris Szagola)

"There's the obvious sort of respiratory illness, cardiovascular issues, vulnerable people with asthma and things like this," Parrington said.

"Then for sure they're going to feel the effects."

During a rehearsal at the stadium for the halftime show, some members of the New York Philharmonic wore masks and some used outdoor-friendly instruments rather than the regular ones they play.

The haze has caused complaints across sports, with athletes critical about the decision to play in hazardous conditions. Before his New York Yankees played at home roughly 20 kilometres from the Meadowlands, manager Aaron Boone said he was not hearing much about the smoke.

"Obviously they're monitoring it to see if it gets any worse," Mr Boone said.

"We'll be communicating with our guys a lot. We're able to test oxygen levels and things like that if guys are having trouble. So, we're paying attention to it, and we'll take the guidance from the league and the weather and the smoke people."

A baseball game in Cleveland between the Guardians and the Pittsburgh Pirates was postponed due to the poor air quality.

ABC Sport will be covering all the World Cup final action via a live blog on Monday morning. Join the team at abc.net.au from 6am.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AP

World.title: Shipping in Strait of Hormuz under attack as US-Iran war heightens
World.content:
The United States has struck bridges in Iran and Tehran has responded by hitting a power and desalination plant in Kuwait.

The attacks, on Friday, local time, saw the two sides risk further escalation of the Iran war by expanding their targets to include infrastructure.

At sea, where the renewed conflict has again cut off energy supplies from the Gulf, US Marines boarded a tanker near the Strait of Hormuz.

Two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after passing through a mined route south of the strait, Iranian media reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Armed men seized another vessel off Yemen, raising concern about security in the Middle East's other big choke point for oil shipments at the mouth of the Red Sea.

Iran's state television quoted the IRGC as saying that until US "aggression" came to an end, it would not be possible to export chemical fertilisers or even a "single drop of oil and gas" from the region.

The interim agreement to end the war collapsed last week when Iran struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz. (Reuters)

US and Iranian attacks risk escalation of war

Washington and Tehran have been testing the limits of escalation since their ceasefire agreement collapsed last week, raising the prospect of a return to all-out war.

After reports of the escalation on Friday, benchmark Brent crude oil prices climbed 3 per cent and were on track for a third consecutive weekly gain, putting political pressure on US President Donald Trump ahead of November congressional elections.

Mr Trump has threatened to launch broad-based air strikes on Iran's infrastructure and has also declined to rule out a ground assault on Iran's coast or islands.

US officials have said attacks on southern Iran are designed in part to give Mr Trump options.

The latest strikes come after Donald Trump threatened to target Iran's civilian infrastructure. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Such moves risk provoking Iran to escalate in turn by hitting the vital infrastructure of vulnerable Gulf states, or having its allies in Yemen further disrupt global energy supplies by attacking shipping from the Red Sea.

Mohsen Rezaei, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, warned on Friday against US escalation or any attempt to seize Iranian territory.

"If US strikes continue for several more days, we will move into a phase of full-scale offensive operations," Mr Rezaei, a former IRGC top commander, told state television.

Iran targets Gulf nations after US strikes airport, bridges, train station

UN Secretary-General António Guterres was concerned about the escalation, particularly over "attacks on civilian infrastructure in Iran and across the region", his spokesperson said.

The US military's Central Command earlier said its targets included "military logistics infrastructure", the first time it mentioned infrastructure in more than a week.

In the latest strikes, Central Command said it re-initiated attacks on Iran for the seventh consecutive night with strikes at 10:30pm Friday, Tehran time.

"The strikes are designed to continue degrading Iranian military capabilities at the Commander in Chief's direction," the statement on X said.

Shortly thereafter, Iranian media reported explosions heard or strikes carried out in the cities of Sirik, Ahvaz and Yazd.

Iranian state media previously said at least five bridges were struck in the south.

Seven people were reported killed in attacks on bridges in the southern port of Bandar Khamir, where the train station was also hit.

An airport was reported hit further east and away from the coast in Iranshahr, in a province bordering Pakistan.

Videos verified by Reuters showed rubble, broken railings and a damaged vehicle on a smashed bridge in Bandar Khamir. One clip showed a fire.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said that three villagers were killed while crossing the Bandar Khamir Bridge, adding that Iran would not allow their blood "to be in vain".

Iran announced attacks on Gulf countries that host US air bases, including Bahrain, Qatar and Kuwait, in addition to a US vessel in the northern Indian Ocean.

The IRGC said it attacked a depot of US drones in Bahrain and destroyed Bahrain's main artificial intelligence centre with ballistic missiles and drones.

The Iranian navy fired a shore-to-sea cruise missile towards what it called a hostile US vessel in the northern Indian Ocean, state news agency IRNA reported on Friday.

Iran's army said the missile launch caused "fear and panic" and forced the vessel to move out of range of Iran's navy.

Authorities in Kuwait said one of the country's power generation and water desalination stations had been hit in an Iranian attack, causing damage, a fire and the disruption of a large number of electricity generation units.

The rich Arab Gulf states depend on plants that produce electricity and remove salt from seawater to make their desert cities habitable.

When Iran hit a Kuwaiti desalination plant on March 30, it was seen as a major escalation.

Last month's interim agreement to end the war has collapsed since July 7, when Iran struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz and the United States responded with air strikes.

Iran has since announced the closure of the strait, and Washington has reimposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.

Reuters

World.title: Irish national admits role in 'nightmare' plan to help alleged criminal flee Australia
World.content:
An Irish national who helped a shadowy international syndicate in a bid to smuggle an alleged fugitive drug trafficker out of Australia via a remote Northern Territory town has pleaded guilty to his role in the million-dollar plot.

Stephen Frances Roche this week pleaded guilty in the NT Supreme Court to attempting to pervert the course of justice, after depositing Hussein Chamas on a Nhulunbuy beach where he was picked up by boat last year.

Court documents released to the ABC detail the scheme to get Mr Chamas out of the country after he fled his NSW bail accommodation in January.

Mr Chamas was on conditional release ahead of his upcoming trial on charges relating to an alleged conspiracy to import a commercial quantity of methamphetamine.

Loading...

The documents allege Mr Chamas allegedly began making plans to evade justice through the "international syndicate" in exchange for $1 million, after his arrest on the drug charges in 2023.

"Operation HARRAKIS is an investigation into an organised criminal group who made arrangements to facilitate the covert removal of individuals from Australia who were the subject of ongoing criminal prosecution," the documents read.

"The investigation identified a complex syndicate who operated covertly across multiple countries.

"The syndicate members responsible for arranging the transport of CHAMAS from Australia referred to him as 'the VIP'."

Alleged drug trafficker absconds from rehab An arrest warrant has been issued for Hussein Chamas, who has absconded from a NSW rehab centre after staff received allegedly forged bail documents.

The documents show in January last year, Roche rented a white campervan in Sydney, which he used to pick Mr Chamas up after he talked his way out of his bail accommodation, and drove him to Arnhem Land.

The documents reveal that on January 25, an NT-based Australian Border Force (ABF) officer spotted a yacht anchored offshore near East Woody Beach with a smaller, blue inflatable boat on board.

"She observed CHAMAS pretending to fish, holding a fishing rod with no fishing line," the documents read.

" As the ABF officer left the beach, she observed CHAMAS use a torch to flash a light towards the yacht, following which a person on board the yacht flashed a light toward the beach. "

The documents allege that later that day, German national Thomas Goertz collected Mr Chamas from the shore in the inflatable boat while his partner, UK citizen Jade Siu Ying Ormiston, took charge of the yacht.

Hussein Chamas was extradited to NSW after his alleged escape plan was foiled. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police )

Once all three were back on board the SV Coconuts, the yacht set sail north, heading out of Australian waters.

It was intercepted by the ABF two days later and Mr Chamas was arrested.

Mr Goertz and Ms Ormiston were also later charged and faced court over their involvement in the enterprise. However they are yet to enter pleas.

Stranded 'in the middle of f***ing nowhere'

At the same time, the documents show Roche was communicating with syndicate members using the codenames "Penfold" and "endangered species", complaining about his mounting expenses after the van broke down during the trip.

"F***ing nightmare to be left like this," he wrote.

"Madness to not plan a more smother [sic] process.

"Also I have to pay for the extra and stay here at the caravan park. And pay for the part to fix the caravan. And the mechanic to do it if he ever shows up wit [sic] the part to do it.

"I have been given money to cover this but it's getting blown out by the day."

Stephen Roche found himself stranded in the remote Arnhem Land town of Nhulunbuy for almost a week after dropping "the VIP" on the beach. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

By January 27, Roche told his handler he was "close to just f***ing off".

"This will ruin me having the caravan under my name, standed [sic] here in the middle of f***ing nowhere," he wrote.

"I might be overreacting, but it's not how it should have gone. And it was all caused by VIP taking over and dictating the plan."

In another conversation with a separate syndicate member, codenamed "Dangermouse", later that day, Roche grumbles about Mr Chamas also complaining "about how much it was all costing him towards the end".

Court documents reveal Stephen Roche was left empty handed for his efforts. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"I couldn't give a f*** what he's complaing [sic] about," Dangermouse replied.

"He won't be complaining when he's free and bangijgva [sic] few birds and drinking a few beers free as a bird. That's just life.

"Brother please trust my words I am the boss here. You will not love loose [sic] a penny you will not he [sic] ripped of [sic].

"Everything thqts [sic] offered cost and monetary valued will be paid."

Police eventually caught up with Roche, still stuck in Nhulunbuy, on February 2 and arrested him before he could receive a promised payment of $30,000 for his trouble.

Defence lawyer points to 'nexus' in poor mental health and offending

Defence lawyer Ian Rowbottam told the court Roche was at a low point psychologically at the time of his offending due to a pre-existing, serious workplace injury.

Ian Rowbottam said his client was struggling with his mental health at the time of his offending. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"As a result of his injury he found himself out of work, in effect," he said.

"[He] lost his house, his relationship.

"These offences occurred at a significantly low time mentally, when he was struggling significantly with issues of mental health, on top of the family breakdown."

"We say there will be a direct nexus able to be found with his mental health at the time of his agreeing to participate in this enterprise."

Roche will return to court for sentencing on September 28.

World.title: 'I didn't feel safe': Mum reveals concerns before childcare closure
World.content:
A Canberra mother had concerns for her daughter's safety at a childcare centre in the city's north-west for more than a year before the ACT regulator ordered it to shut.

Alison Sweeney, whose daughter attends Edge Early Learning in Higgins, said she was not surprised the Children's Education and Care Assurance (CECA) issued the centre with a notice to close.

"We've been having issues now for a couple of years with the centre, director after director, with the high staff turnover, and obviously incidents with my daughter," Ms Sweeney said.

" It got to the point where I didn't particularly feel safe with her going to school each day. "

She said her daughter, Blake, had wandered from the centre more than once, had her hair cut with adult scissors and knocked out her front teeth while playing on equipment.

"She's now without teeth until her new ones come through, which shouldn't be until next year," she said.

"Do better. They've let an entire community down, and I just think it's appalling."

Alison Sweeney's daughter, Blake, knocked her front teeth out while playing on equipment. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Regulator cracks down after incident

The regulator issued Edge Early Learning in Higgins with a notice to close for a month until August 13, accusing it of failing to respond to a serious medical incident involving a child.

"CECA is currently investigating a range of issues arising from the incident," a spokesperson said.

Some families received an email from Edge Early Learning's CEO Chris Chambers on Thursday night, informing them the centre would abruptly shut.

"We are disappointed that CECA has now required the centre to close immediately," Mr Chambers said in the email.

He said the centre had terminated a staff member over the incident and suspended others while an investigation was underway.

"While we are pleased that the child is OK, I want to be very clear that the educator's response to the incident was completely unacceptable."

Edge Early Learning contacted families who send their children to its Higgins centre on Thursday. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Worsening quality of care

Ms Sweeney said she had noticed a sharp decline in the quality of care at the centre when Edge Early Learning took over from the former operator Little Penguins.

At the time, her eldest child, Nixon, was attending the centre.

"As soon as Edge took over, there was a noticeable change instantly," she said.

Ms Sweeney, who runs a small business, now has to take her daughter to work because she is unable to work from home.

"It leaves me in a situation where I have to take her to work with me every day, which is not ideal at all," she said.

She said the centre's sudden closure would also impact her daughter's friendships and she would not get the chance to graduate properly.

"I may not even put her back in daycare," Ms Sweeney said.

'We need to tighten regulations': Emerson

Edge Early Learning is a large childcare provider that operates centres around the country, including in South Australia and Queensland.

Earlier this month, the South Australian childcare regulator closed the company's centre north of Adelaide in Gawler East, after a child was served food with an allergen the centre knew about.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson, an advocate for stronger childcare regulation in the ACT, backed the regulator's decision to suspend the Higgins centre.

"I think it's good to see the regulator taking firm action," Mr Emerson said.

Thomas Emerson is calling for stronger regulation of the childcare sector in the ACT. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

He said that centre had a history of incidents related to poor supervision, inappropriate discipline, and an educator working without a Working with Vulnerable People check.

"It's really disappointing," he said.

The member for Kurrajong said the latest incident was another example of why the ACT government needed to increase standards of care in the sector and better support smaller community operators.

"What I haven't seen is enough support for the smaller local providers that are run by people who are part of our community," he said.

"We need to tighten regulations."

World.title: These lemurs like to 'move it, move it' to the sound of a harp
World.content:
Most musicians would be disappointed if their performances were met with silence.

But not Alison Ware.

Every fortnight, the Canberra harp therapist performs for some of her most attentive audience members — rhinos, lemurs, lions and a school of Amazonian fish at the National Zoo and Aquarium.

For the past five years, Ms Ware has been volunteering at the zoo, using music as a form of animal enrichment.

Alison Ware as been volunteering at the National Zoo and Aquarium for five years. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

Armed with several different harps of varying sizes, she moves between enclosures, carefully adapting her performance to suit each animal.

"It's really like humans, some days we feel like music and some days we don't," she said.

Alison spends time watching each animal, adjusting the tempo, tone and volume of the music as she gauges their response.

"The primates tend to like the smaller harp with a lighter sound and the rhinos like deeper tones with a larger harp," she said.

Curious lemurs come up close when Ms Ware plays the harp inside their enclosure. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

Some animals wander over to investigate. Others simply settle where they are, seemingly soothed by the gentle melodies.

But Ms Ware's audience extends beyond furry and feathered animals. Even the aquarium's South American pacu often swim toward the music as Ms Ware plays.

"Most of the animals fall asleep or they'll come closer to listen to the music," she said.

The South American pacu often swim towards the music as Ms Ware plays. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

A calming soundtrack for curious lemurs

Head primate keeper Olivia Ware, who is also Alison's daughter, said her mother's visits had become a welcome addition to the lemurs' enrichment program.

"Of course, being in the zoo, the lemurs already hear a lot of different sounds," she said.

" But it's nice to bring the harp in as it's such a unique auditory enrichment. It's also very calming for them as well. "

Head primate keeper Olivia Ware says the lemurs have shown a preference for the smaller of the two harps. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

Olivia Ware said the lemurs' response was often immediate.

"Normally they just sit in the sun, curl up in a ball and listen to the harp," she said.

Over time, the keepers have discovered the lemurs have their own musical preferences.

"They tend to like the smaller of the two harps. Sometimes the larger harp can be a little bit scary for them," Olivia Ware said.

Alison Ware plays a number of different harps of varying sizes. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

Sharing music beyond people

Away from the zoo, Alison Ware has spent more than 20 years working as a clinical music therapist, using the harp to support patients and families in palliative care wards, emergency rooms and aged care facilities.

She said bringing her music to animals felt like a natural extension of that work.

"I've always enjoyed spending time with animals," she said.

" I use the harp in health care, and I really felt I wanted to do something a little bit different with my music. "

Ms Ware's playing attracts the attention of an oryx at the zoo. (ABC News: Sarah Grieb)

Five years in, Ms Ware said she still looked forward to every visit, never quite knowing which animals would be in the mood for a concert.

"I absolutely love it," she said.

World.title: With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction
World.content:
NationalWACity life With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction Cameron Myles July 18, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has been a turbulent time for writers’ festivals over the past few years. In South Australia, the controversy with the Adelaide Writers’ Week boycotts and eventual cancellation are well documented. In Bendigo last year, dozens of authors quit the writers’ festival, leading to the cancellation of the opening night gala. Children’s author Mem Fox will be at this year’s Festival of Fiction. Meanwhile, in WA, it was announced in 2024 that the Perth Writers Weekend was to move to a standalone event to be held in spring 2026, having previously been part of the Perth Festival. It is against this cultural backdrop that another festival returns to Perth’s literary scene this year, with its focus remaining firmly on the fiction aisles.



Perth’s Festival of Fiction has announced its line-up for 2026, with names on the billing including beloved children’s author Mem Fox, award-winning writer Christos Tsiolkas, alongside the likes of Sally Hepworth and Kate Morton. Christos Tsiolkas has taken the tired ploy of the self-referential text and reinvigorated it. Eddie Jim Festival director Tess Woods said the appeal of festivals was clear – they offered a reprieve, an ability to get out and engage with those who write the books we love, or even loathe. “We’re getting more and more divisive, and we’re seeing that you know across social media and in politics,” she said. “And there’s very little nuance left now on both sides of the spectrum.



“So festivals are an opportunity for us to see each other face-to-face, to get away from our keyboards, and to see that, you know, maybe an author whose political opinion you don’t agree with, you see them on stage and you’re like, ‘You know this is a human, this is a person with feelings, who laughs and who has a family’.” Related Article Literature Adelaide Festival attendance halved in wake of Writers’ Week drama The benefit extends beyond the experience of readers. Writers, Woods notes, spend a lot of time by themselves, and festivals are a good way to meet others and expand their networks. For Woods, who will finish up as director after this year’s festival, the prioritising of fiction was both a much-needed point of difference and a drawcard. “I felt that genre fiction writers were often excluded from the more traditional mainstream literary festivals,” she said.



“They throw them a bone. You would have, your two or three crime writers, or your two or three, general fiction writers, and then they were mostly dominated by literary fiction, poets, non-fiction, journalists, memoir [writers]. “And so I felt that the books that you’re seeing in Big W and Dymocks that are making up that top 10, that are keeping the publishing industry alive, that your average punter is going out to buy - your crime and your romance and fantasy - they just weren’t represented enough at the big literary festivals.” The festival has two Miles Franklin award-winners on the billing – Siang Lu and Sofie Laguna – as well as Toni Jordan, who was longlisted for the prestigious award. And Fox, the author of Australian children’s classics such as Possum Magic, Time for Bed, and Where is the Green Sheep will be holding workshops on something she is no doubt an expert in – “how to find the right words”. While major challenges revolving around freedom of speech and politics made headlines, Woods said the ever-present threat to writers’ festivals was funding.



“We have run this festival three years now with a committee of 20 volunteers, unpaid, and it’s just been a labor of love,” she said. “We’re very lucky that the City of Joondalup have generously sponsored us, so we’ve got that Joondalup funding, but it’s just not enough to make it keep going. “For the last two years, we haven’t had a Perth Writers Festival. I think we’re the only state in Australia after Adelaide had theirs canceled that hasn’t got one.” The Festival of Fiction will return to Edith Cowan University’s Joondalup campus on November 21-22.

World.title: ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau threatens to quit British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty
World.content:
Updated SportGolfBritish Open ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau threatens to quit British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty Tom Decent Updated July 18, 2026 — 9:54am ,first published 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Southport: Controversy has erupted at the British Open, with American star Bryson DeChambeau threatening to withdraw from the tournament after being hit with a two-shot penalty for “improving the area” of his intended backswing. It comes as DeChambeau’s agent claimed his client wasn’t a cheat and argued he wasn’t trying to gain an unfair advantage during an incident that has divided the golf world. Bryson DeChambeau speaks with officials after his round on Friday at the British Open. X After carding a four-under 66 on Friday, DeChambeau walked off the 18th green at Royal Birkdale in outright second on seven-under, behind Australia’s Lucas Herbert, who shot a record-equalling 62 to head to the weekend at eight-under. But after signing his card, DeChambeau was approached by rules officials over an incident on the fifth hole earlier in the day.



Playing his second shot from thick rough, television footage appeared to show DeChambeau walking around the area of his ball before taking his shot, with officials believing his actions improved the area where his club would swing. There was a suggestion he stamped down grass behind the ball. Although the ball itself never moved, the rules of golf prohibit players from improving the area of an intended stance or swing. DeChambeau and his agent Brett Falkoff (left) on a controversial evening at the British Open. Getty Images A visibly frustrated DeChambeau was taken back to the fifth hole by officials, where he remonstrated with tournament staff and appeared to tell decision-makers he would not continue in the championship. His manager was also present during the dramatic exchange broadcast on live television. Shortly afterwards, amid a crush of television cameras and waiting reporters, tournament rules official Grant Moir confirmed DeChambeau had been docked two shots. His bogey on the 5th hole would become a triple bogey seven.



The penalty dropped DeChambeau from seven-under to five-under, leaving him tied for fifth rather than second. “Bryson has been penalised two strokes for inadvertently improving the area of intended back swing on fifth hole,” Moir said. Grant Moir, executive director of governance at The R&A, speaks to the media regarding a two-stoke penalty assessed against DeChambeau. Getty Images “Ruling one restricts what a player may do to improve any of the protected conditions affecting the stroke and this includes the area of the player’s intended swing. “So an improvement means to alter one or more of the conditions affecting the stroke so that the player gains a potential advantage for the stroke. Now, I’ll stress that this applies even when the action is accidental, as it was in Bryson’s case.”



When asked by reporters as he walked away whether he would return for Saturday’s third round, DeChambeau stopped short of giving any assurance. He instead headed to the practice range, where he began hitting balls as darkness fell over Royal Birkdale. DeChambeau’s agent Brett Falkoff said he would decide on Saturday morning whether he would continue playing but said his 32-year-old client is angry. “He’s a lot of things. He’s not a cheater,” Falkoff said. “He’s a big boy. He’ll see how he feels. But he certainly feels he was unfairly penalised.” DeChambeau is a popular player on tour but also divisive among fans, having defected to LIV Golf on a lucrative deal worth more than $100 million (USD).



Herbert was supposed to be paired with DeChambeau on Saturday but the latest drama means he will instead play his third round with Jackson Suber at 3.50pm local time (12.50am AEST). DeChambeau is listed to tee off at 3.30pm (12.30am) but if he pulled out of the tournament it would be unprecedented scenes. World.title: Ronnie Di Stasio on closing the pioneering Cafe Di Stasio after 38 years
World.content:
As the sun sets on one of Melbourne’s most influential Italian restaurants, its creator and his partner Mallory Wall remember the chaos, the hard times and St Kilda of old.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Restaurateur Rinaldo Di Stasio pulled an all-nighter on Tuesday as champagne-fuelled celebrations for the sale of Cafe Di Stasio morphed into a 5am World Cup watch party. His St Kilda hive of Italian good times this week passed into the hands of one of its former chefs, Nathan Presley, who will reopen it in August as a seafood restaurant. After 38 years, the Campari-soaked reign of 71-year-old Di Stasio over the Fitzroy Street dining room that helped propel Melbourne’s restaurant scene onto the global stage is over. 1 / 11 Regulars loved the restaurant's hedonistic atmosphere as much as its food. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 2 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio at the St Kilda restaurant in 1991. Mario Borg 3 / 11 Cafe Di Stasio in St Kilda circa 2012. Supplied 4 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio built a reputation for long lunches and late nights at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 5 / 11 Old s for Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 6 / 11 One  shows Rinaldo Di Stasio with shirtless waiter Benito Rega. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 7 / 11 The restaurant had a clubby, intimate atmosphere. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall 8 / 11 Rinaldo di Stasio at Cafe Di Stasio in 1990. Supplied 9 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall, circa 2006, in the dining room. Eamon Gallagher 10 / 11 Mallory Wall and Ronnie Di Stasio in the courtyard of Di Stasio Carlton in 2021. Kristoffer Paulsen 11 / 11 Rinaldo Di Stasio (left) with chef Valerio Nucci and Mallory Wall at Cafe Di Stasio circa 1996. Craig Abraham Previous Slide Next Slide “When we walked out at 2am on the last night two weeks ago, I was not sad,” he says. “St Kilda is not the same. The time was probably overdue for us to leave.” It was a 40-degree day on January 11, 1988, when Cafe Di Stasio opened with no air-conditioning and 45 diners for lunch. Back then, the hottest ticket in town was Lynch’s Restaurant in South Yarra, with its starched-tablecloth take on French cuisine. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up There were great Italian restaurants in Melbourne, testaments to waves of Italian immigrants: the grand Florentino on Bourke Street and Mario’s Restaurant by the sea in Brighton. But there was nothing quite like Cafe Di Stasio.



‘The restaurant was designed for gossip, affairs, fun. Eating was just part of it.’ Rinaldo Di Stasio on Cafe Di Stasio Designed by longtime friend and collaborator, architect Allan Powell, the walls were hung with contemporary Australian art by Bill Henson, who also frequented the restaurant, and the staff wore raffish white jackets and bowties. The menu channelled an Italy that Di Stasio, born in Melbourne to Neapolitan immigrants, had soaked in during what he calls his “PhD year” living in Naples and Rome. Dishes like beef carpaccio with rocket were unfamiliar to people. Jason Lui, general manager of Flower Drum and a regular diner, describes the food as “Italian like no one else was doing it: simple and authentic”. “You went wanting to eat just a bowl of pasta,” says Lui. “But you ordered starters, dessert, champagne. You spent three times as much as you wanted to, but you left happy.” Mallory Wall (rear) briefs waiters before service at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall Di Stasio sums up the appeal of the restaurant as “genteel chaos”.



“There are two things people want in restaurants they don’t get at home: theatre and someone else to do the dishes. Women would sometimes say to me, ‘I could cook this at home’. I’d say, ‘No, you could cook much better, but you’d have to wash the dishes. And it wouldn’t be as fun’.” It was a hit from day one. Jill Dupleix, recipe writer, food editor and St Kilda resident at the time, went the first day for a coffee, realised it was a restaurant not a cafe, and went back for lunch, then again for dinner. “It was a pivotal restaurant for Melbourne,” she says. “It was like suddenly the grown-ups had arrived, there was a new standard in town. Ronnie cared deeply about what it was to be an Italian restaurateur and unleashed that upon the world.” Before St Kilda, Di Stasio had presided over the 500-seat, mosaic-tiled Rosati restaurant in Flinders Lane. It was the first restaurant to open on the CBD thoroughfare which has since flourished into a dining mecca. After owning the flamboyant venue for three years, Di Stasio’s relationship with his business partner imploded and he left. Ten days later, in September 1987, he signed the lease of what would become Cafe Di Stasio. “People thought I was nuts when I opened Rosati. No one paid attention to the city’s laneways. But it was one block back from Collins Street and instead of paying $3000 a week rent, I was paying $800. When I went to St Kilda, which was a pretty down-and-out suburb, people thought I was nuts again. But I cracked it.” Cafe Di Stasio in St Kilda circa 2012.



He brought with him a Rolodex of fans who filled the restaurant from lunch to dinner, along with St Kilda locals: “The artists, drag girls, the prostitutes.” “The restaurant was designed for gossip, affairs, fun. Eating was just part of it,” he says. It certainly was chaos. Two years after opening, Di Stasio was standing on the footpath outside when he spotted a woman familiar to him. She was Mallory Wall, a 21-year-old who used to wag school in Mentone to frequent Rosati, and now lived nearby after working in London for two years. He offered her a job and she started almost immediately. Her second night in the dining room was Valentine’s Day. “I looked at the bookings diary,” Wall recalls. “There were 130 people booked in. We were a 70-seat restaurant. And they were all coming at 8 o’clock.” Wall worked on bringing some order to the chaos and she and Di Stasio focused on their complementary skills in business.



“We discovered how to run a restaurant together, and discovered each other as well,” she says. Stars started swinging through the front door with its trademark bronze hands. The Rolling Stones, Nick Cave (a regular), Kevin Spacey, U2, Steve Martin, Barry Humphries, Marianne Faithfull. “It was madness. We’d push back the tables and dance in the dining room; lunch would run into dinner and then go all night,” Di Stasio says. Rinaldo Di Stasio built a reputation for long lunches and late nights at Cafe Di Stasio. Courtesy Rinaldo Di Stasio and Mallory Wall At least once a week he would jump on a table and spray the room with champagne. “It was always French, even though I tried to get him to use the cheap stuff,” says Wall. It did take a toll on Di Stasio. Seven years in, instead of opening another, larger restaurant, he bought 32-hectares in the Yarra Valley and started creating a house, designed again by Powell, and a vineyard.

World.title: I never liked small dogs. But then along came Ferdie
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsPets Opinion I never liked small dogs. But then along came Ferdie Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist July 18, 2026 — 9:30am

July 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This is a story about changing yourself. George Bernard Shaw said, “Those who cannot change their minds cannot change anything.” We live in a time, seemingly, of deepening entrenchment. If Shaw was right, this rigidity is not strength but powerlessness. Malcolm Knox with his dog Ferdie, a Prague ratter. I never liked small dogs. Growing up, we had medium-sized dogs, proper dogs. We had one seriously big dog: my brother, a vet who should have known his stuff, brought home a beagle pup that didn’t stop growing until he’d become a giant fox hound, who looked like Snoopy but was bigger than his kennel. Years later, my family adopted Bruce, a rescue blue heeler-kelpie cross, another proper dog with a beautiful loyal intelligence, a classic best mate. Since 2021 when he died, I was mourning Bruce. His collar still hung from the car’s rear vision mirror. Our children moved out. My beloved kept telling me I needed a dog, but I couldn’t replace Bruce (or, for that matter, the children). I didn’t replace him. Instead, I changed.



Plenty of people dislike small dogs, and I was one of them. As for very small dogs, which even the pet industry classifies as toys rather than actual dogs? Bulgy-eyed, yappy, precious little tyrants who travel in handbags: you might as well get a ferret. I didn’t want another dog anyway. Ferdie thinks I’m pretty awesome, like my kids did when they were about nine. Sometimes change comes because something deep inside you says if you don’t do it, you are giving up on more than you know. The dog change was like that. We dogsat a friend’s chihuahua, and he was unexpectedly loveable. My wife began haunting chihuahua rescue sites. A certain momentum built. Of course, it wasn’t really about a dog; it was about whether one of us had become stuck. Danger Mouse, as he was known, was having trouble getting adopted. Two years old, black with tan markings, he had behavioural problems after being raised in a family with 11 children. Yes, such families still exist, and this tiny dog had grown up with wave after wave of two-legged monsters in his face. He’d developed severe anxieties. Great. When you procrastinate for long enough, it can be best to let the universe have its way. Every good story starts with “yes”. So here I was, giving up and changing before I could get in my own way and unchange.



Because we thought he was a chihuahua, we gave him a Spanish name. Ferdie didn’t act like a chihuahua though: no barking, no aggro towards other dogs, a lusty appetite and a rather more handsome longer snout and smaller eyes offset by a weirdly big set of ears. He was also, if possible, smaller than a chihuahua. Some kind of miniature pinscher? Then during a morning walk, this random woman said, “Is that a Prague ratter?” Excuse me, we don’t think so. Did she just call our dog a rat? On a city walk, a young drinker in a pub yelled out, “Oi, how’s ya Prague ratter!” What the actual? An imposter chihuahua? We looked up Prague ratters and they looked like Ferdie. The behavioural tics – the non-barking, the ease around other dogs, the food obsession, the devotion to curling up in your lap – were pure Prague ratter. There aren’t many in Australia and only Ferdie knows how he got here, but he’s telling no tales. Conveniently, Ferdinand can also be a Central European name. The best thing about toy dogs, what I never realised because I never liked them, is how much pleasure they give strangers. Honestly, it’s like walking around with Timothée Chalamet on a leash. The guy’s a superstar. Kids, adults, old folk, it doesn’t matter: Ferdie puts smiles on faces. You can’t go one block without being stopped by people who want to pat him, talk to him, ask you about him. Passers-by say, “Look, he’s so cute!” and they’re not talking about me. As charismatic as Bruce was, he was a D-list celebrity compared with this bloke. It’s nice to make people happy without doing anything to earn it.



Related Article Pets After three days on a ledge, and two at the vet, Elbie is just fine. For her owner, it’s a different story He’s become the most photographed member of the family. Beyond cuteness, why does a dog complete the picture? In a new book about dogs in art, The Dog’s Gaze, historian Thomas Laqueur details how the first family member Odysseus meets, returning to Ithaca in Homer’s Odyssey, is his dog Argos: “Look! – he wagged his tail and both his ears went flat.” Centuries later, the photographer Richard Avedon said his parents always borrowed a dog for family portraits. “They bring their world into ours, which is perhaps how they make us feel less lonely as a species,” Laqueur writes. “They humanise humans.” Ferdie is gracious about his work to humanise humans. Like a Sam Neill of dogs, he takes it in his stride and is happy to have made others happy. You wouldn’t call him gregarious, and he’s actually hoping they have food for him, but he has none of that small-dog Napoleon syndrome. He gets on with fellow dogs except the odd greyhound who eyes him off like he’s an hors d’oeuvre. Out in the world, he’s a lover, not a fighter. Different story at home, where he seems to think that I need a bodyguard. In a recent American YouGov survey, 95 per cent of dog owners said their pet gave them unconditional love. Ferdie thinks I’m pretty awesome, like my kids did when they were about nine, but he also thinks I need close protection. He thinks any visitor has come to hurt or steal me. He has bitten my brother, my son, my daughter, my friends, my mother-in-law, the neighbours and the oven man. Visitors/intruders/hostile alien life-forms need to pass this trial before he settles down. Prague ratters don’t take well to types of discipline that work for other dogs: we tried using a water spray to correct his behaviour and he nearly took our arm off. As a last resort, there are muzzles small enough to fit over one of your fingers. Nobody’s perfect. He hates being left alone but at least he doesn’t take it out on the furniture. He’s more or less house-trained but isn’t above the occasional excitement wee or poo; he just prefers to do his ablutions out on the Walk of Fame.



In that same YouGov survey, 66 per cent of owners thought their dogs’ intelligence was above-average and 27 per cent average, leaving just 7 per cent who thought their dogs were below average. Everyone scores an A. I’ll admit Ferdie is probably among the 7 per cent. What is dog intelligence worth anyway, when you put so many smiles on faces? Having changed, there was one other change to cope with. Chihuahuas’ life expectancy can be 20-plus years, whereas Prague ratters only live to 12 or so. So we probably won’t have him as long as expected. More reason to make the most of things while they last. By that time, I’ll have become that most risible of human beings, the “toy-dog person”. I might have reckoned with other new realities. If you can change not only your views but your affinities, not only your likes but your loves, not only your preferences but your weaknesses, then you can still change the world beyond your door. Malcolm Knox is a journalist, author and columnist. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here

World.title: From garbo to Italian job: Paenga-Amosa’s lesson in resilience for struggling Wallabies
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies From garbo to Italian job: Paenga-Amosa’s lesson in resilience for struggling Wallabies Jonathan Drennan July 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After nine losses in their past 10 Test matches, the Wallabies are being forced to learn about resilience. Hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa is well qualified to be their teacher. Before turning professional, he taught a class in mental strength to teenagers in western Sydney and would wake up at 4am to work as a garbage man across Redfern in the depths of winter. Brandon Paenga-Amosa of the Wallabies celebrates scoring a try earlier in the game. Getty Images That background gives Paenga-Amosa a different mindset than most heading into Saturday’s clash with Italy in Perth. “It’s just perspective ahead of this game. I could be digging holes out the back. I could be running behind the garbage truck getting a bit of bin juice on me here and there,” Paenga-Amosa said.



“Those jobs definitely shaped my perspective on the world and just life in general. But with that being said, I wouldn’t change anything about the route that I took. “Even as a dad, to be able to teach my kids that sometimes what you want takes a bit of work.” Brandon-Paenga Amosa acknowledging the work of teammate Angus Bell Getty Images Paenga-Amosa was never picked for representative sides as a schoolboy and worked as a garbage man, a teacher, a gardener, a trampoline attendant and a labourer while playing for Southern Districts in the Shute Shield. His shot at professional rugby came in 2018 at the Reds. He spent three years in Brisbane and then three seasons in France with Montpellier before returning to Australia to play for the Western Force.



In the Wallabies’ defeat against France last Saturday, Paenga-Amosa was outstanding, coming off the bench after three minutes and finishing the game after Josh Nasser was ruled out after a head knock. He playfully sledged the French front row in their native language during the scrum and after scoring a try, but got tongue-tied as fatigue set in. Even in the dark moments that come when plying your trade as a Test hooker, Paenga-Amosa regularly pops up from scrums and mauls with a wide smile on his face. The Western Force player always wants to show his appreciation for his teammates during the toughest of times on the field. “I always look at the cup half-full rather than half-empty; I love getting around the boys, and I love big moments in games,” Paenga-Amosa said. “When we win those moments, like a scrum penalty or a try, there aren’t many things in the world that can beat that feeling. “For me, rugby’s more than just the game ... There’s a strong brotherhood in the squad, and honestly these last two losses [against France and Ireland] have actually brought us together even closer as a team, which is important.”



Related Article Wallabies Wallabies’ playmaker carousel spins on as Cooper questions Lolesio snub Against Italy, Paenga-Amosa will face a squad full of confidence after a strong Six Nations campaign, but he believes a win for the Wallabies will create momentum that is desperately needed ahead of new coach Les Kiss taking over. “Once we get that one win, it’ll snowball into more wins. We deserve it, I feel we beat ourselves in the last two games,” Paenga-Amosa said. “It would be really good for us as a squad to not beat ourselves in this next game, to actually earn the win that we deserve and put together a performance that not just we’re proud of, but our supporters, our country and our nation are proud of as well.”

World.title: Why are far too many Wallabies missing far too many minutes?
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion Why are far too many Wallabies missing far too many minutes? Paul Cully Rugby columnist July 18, 2026 — 9:30am

July 18, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In the normal world, Carter Gordon or Tom Lynagh would be leading the Wallabies against Italy in Perth on Saturday, ably backed up by Ben Donaldson. But long-suffering Wallabies fans haven’t had the luxury of living in the normal world for at least four years when it comes to injuries. Loading In late 2022, then Rugby Australia chief executive Andy Marinos said an “alarming” cluster of ruptured Achilles injuries within four months would be scrutinised in an independent review. Additionally, about 40 other separate injuries that ruled players out of Tests would be probed. Yet, four years later Gordon, Lynagh and Donaldson all either have active calf injuries or are recovering from them.



The straw that broke the camel’s back this week was Italy winger Louis Lynagh’s revelation that brother Tom had missed almost the entire Super Rugby season with the all-too-familiar lower limb ailment. “He [Tom] had two back-to-back calf tears,” Louis told the Herald. “I thought it was just constant niggles, like hamstring and calf issues, but it was more serious this time around. Ben Donaldson reacts to his missed goal against Ireland. Getty Images “He seems to be doing well now, touch wood. He ran today [in Perth] and went to the gym, so he seems to be back on top of it.” If this is accurate, and there is no reason to dispute it, Australian rugby has a big problem.



No Wallabies coach will be able to do anything with this pool of players if they can’t stay fit. This is a fundamental issue that is a higher priority than tactics, selection, culture or whatever lens you might apply to performances. Wallabies playmaker Carter Gordon is out injured. Getty Images In fact, the biggest risk Joe Schmidt has taken this week is not selecting Declan Meredith at No.10, but putting Donaldson on the bench. If Donaldson blows his calf, the Wallabies’ next Test - with new coach Les Kiss in charge - against Japan on August 8 starts to look very tricky. It is hard to fathom these injuries to Gordon, 25, Donaldson, 27, and Lynagh, 23. Calf issues are an old man’s injury, not three blokes who should be as fit and resilient as they’ll ever be during their lifetimes.



Yes, injuries do happen. We saw that during Super Rugby Pacific with the unlucky Western Force halfback Henry Robertson, who did his ACL. More pertinently, Waratahs and Wallabies halfback Jake Gordon did his Achilles (yet another one) in round 16 against the Force. Another Wallaby, Jake Gordon is out injured. Getty Images But Gordon is 33 years old, and you can sort of live with that one due to his age and the sheer number of kilometres he has accumulated during his career. However, no one should accept - at least unquestionably - the calf injuries to the No. 10s, which come on the back of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii missing a big chunk of the Waratahs’ season with his own soft tissue problem (hamstring).



Another perspective Australian rugby They led NSW to their only Super Rugby title. Now they are back in blue Force’s Zac Lomax’s significant groin injury, also revealed this week, feels more coincidental but is still a concern given the Wallabies’ recent track record. It begs the question of how players are being trained, or managed, because we are not seeing this recurring level of soft tissue and lower limb injuries in other Test nations. Given the length of the European club seasons, it was notable to see France field Romain Ntamack and Matthieu Jalibert against the Wallabies in Brisbane, while Scotland had access to Finn Russell against the Springboks, and England lined up stars Fin Smith and Marcus Smith against Fiji. Ntamack has missed a fair bit of rugby in recent years, but those long absences were primarily due to structural injuries (ACL), while Ireland’s absent No. 10 Jack Crowley is dealing with an unusual blood vessel issue in his leg.



Ironically, Italy are dealing with plenty of wear and tear themselves and have named a much-changed team without classy centre Tommaso Menoncello to face the Wallabies. That means the Wallabies should get the job done against the No.10-ranked side in the world. But the bigger picture is that far too many good players are missing far too many Wallabies minutes, and there doesn’t seem to be much light at the end of that tunnel.

World.title: My ex-partner wants to try tuning-fork therapy. Should I tell anyone?
World.content:
Q: My partner broke up with me. I suggested couples counselling. She said she has her own supports in place: tuning-fork therapy, numerology and rebirthing. Friends are asking why we’re not attending counselling. Can I tell them about the tuning forks? V.D., Burwood, VIC

Photo: Illustration by Simon Letch

A: Tuning-fork therapy is new to me. I looked into it and, apparently, it’s a healing technique that uses vibrating tuning forks to relieve emotional trauma. This may work, except the best way to make a tuning fork vibrate is to whack it really hard on your knee, so, after several sessions, you might be emotionally healed, but you’ll be limping to an orthopaedic surgeon to get a kneecap reconstruction.

Anyway, I’ll start by saying that I’m really sorry to hear that your partner broke up with you, and I can sense you’re hoping to get back together again – but because you suggested trying couples counselling with a trained professional while she’s choosing to absorb the vibrations of a pronged fork, interpret occult number patterns and recreate her own birth by pretending a backyard hot tub is her mother’s birth canal, I wonder if maybe, just maybe, the two of you weren’t the most ideal match to begin with.

World.title: With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction
World.content:
NationalWACity life With a beloved children’s author on the bill, this Perth festival isn’t afraid to sort fact from fiction Cameron Myles July 18, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It has been a turbulent time for writers’ festivals over the past few years. In South Australia, the controversy with the Adelaide Writers’ Week boycotts and eventual cancellation are well documented. In Bendigo last year, dozens of authors quit the writers’ festival, leading to the cancellation of the opening night gala. Children’s author Mem Fox will be at this year’s Festival of Fiction. Meanwhile, in WA, it was announced in 2024 that the Perth Writers Weekend was to move to a standalone event to be held in spring 2026, having previously been part of the Perth Festival. It is against this cultural backdrop that another festival returns to Perth’s literary scene this year, with its focus remaining firmly on the fiction aisles.



Perth’s Festival of Fiction has announced its line-up for 2026, with names on the billing including beloved children’s author Mem Fox, award-winning writer Christos Tsiolkas, alongside the likes of Sally Hepworth and Kate Morton. Christos Tsiolkas has taken the tired ploy of the self-referential text and reinvigorated it. Eddie Jim Festival director Tess Woods said the appeal of festivals was clear – they offered a reprieve, an ability to get out and engage with those who write the books we love, or even loathe. “We’re getting more and more divisive, and we’re seeing that you know across social media and in politics,” she said. “And there’s very little nuance left now on both sides of the spectrum.



“So festivals are an opportunity for us to see each other face-to-face, to get away from our keyboards, and to see that, you know, maybe an author whose political opinion you don’t agree with, you see them on stage and you’re like, ‘You know this is a human, this is a person with feelings, who laughs and who has a family’.” Related Article Literature Adelaide Festival attendance halved in wake of Writers’ Week drama The benefit extends beyond the experience of readers. Writers, Woods notes, spend a lot of time by themselves, and festivals are a good way to meet others and expand their networks. For Woods, who will finish up as director after this year’s festival, the prioritising of fiction was both a much-needed point of difference and a drawcard. “I felt that genre fiction writers were often excluded from the more traditional mainstream literary festivals,” she said.



“They throw them a bone. You would have, your two or three crime writers, or your two or three, general fiction writers, and then they were mostly dominated by literary fiction, poets, non-fiction, journalists, memoir [writers]. “And so I felt that the books that you’re seeing in Big W and Dymocks that are making up that top 10, that are keeping the publishing industry alive, that your average punter is going out to buy - your crime and your romance and fantasy - they just weren’t represented enough at the big literary festivals.” The festival has two Miles Franklin award-winners on the billing – Siang Lu and Sofie Laguna – as well as Toni Jordan, who was longlisted for the prestigious award. And Fox, the author of Australian children’s classics such as Possum Magic, Time for Bed, and Where is the Green Sheep will be holding workshops on something she is no doubt an expert in – “how to find the right words”. While major challenges revolving around freedom of speech and politics made headlines, Woods said the ever-present threat to writers’ festivals was funding.



“We have run this festival three years now with a committee of 20 volunteers, unpaid, and it’s just been a labor of love,” she said. “We’re very lucky that the City of Joondalup have generously sponsored us, so we’ve got that Joondalup funding, but it’s just not enough to make it keep going. “For the last two years, we haven’t had a Perth Writers Festival. I think we’re the only state in Australia after Adelaide had theirs canceled that hasn’t got one.” The Festival of Fiction will return to Edith Cowan University’s Joondalup campus on November 21-22.

World.title: ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau threatens to quit British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty
World.content:
Updated SportGolfBritish Open ‘He’s not a cheater’: DeChambeau threatens to quit British Open as controversy erupts over two-shot penalty Tom Decent Updated July 18, 2026 — 9:54am ,first published 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Southport: Controversy has erupted at the British Open, with American star Bryson DeChambeau threatening to withdraw from the tournament after being hit with a two-shot penalty for “improving the area” of his intended backswing. It comes as DeChambeau’s agent claimed his client wasn’t a cheat and argued he wasn’t trying to gain an unfair advantage during an incident that has divided the golf world. Bryson DeChambeau speaks with officials after his round on Friday at the British Open. X After carding a four-under 66 on Friday, DeChambeau walked off the 18th green at Royal Birkdale in outright second on seven-under, behind Australia’s Lucas Herbert, who shot a record-equalling 62 to head to the weekend at eight-under. But after signing his card, DeChambeau was approached by rules officials over an incident on the fifth hole earlier in the day.



Playing his second shot from thick rough, television footage appeared to show DeChambeau walking around the area of his ball before taking his shot, with officials believing his actions improved the area where his club would swing. There was a suggestion he stamped down grass behind the ball. Although the ball itself never moved, the rules of golf prohibit players from improving the area of an intended stance or swing. DeChambeau and his agent Brett Falkoff (left) on a controversial evening at the British Open. Getty Images A visibly frustrated DeChambeau was taken back to the fifth hole by officials, where he remonstrated with tournament staff and appeared to tell decision-makers he would not continue in the championship. His manager was also present during the dramatic exchange broadcast on live television. Shortly afterwards, amid a crush of television cameras and waiting reporters, tournament rules official Grant Moir confirmed DeChambeau had been docked two shots. His bogey on the 5th hole would become a triple bogey seven.



The penalty dropped DeChambeau from seven-under to five-under, leaving him tied for fifth rather than second. “Bryson has been penalised two strokes for inadvertently improving the area of intended back swing on fifth hole,” Moir said. Grant Moir, executive director of governance at The R&A, speaks to the media regarding a two-stoke penalty assessed against DeChambeau. Getty Images “Ruling one restricts what a player may do to improve any of the protected conditions affecting the stroke and this includes the area of the player’s intended swing. “So an improvement means to alter one or more of the conditions affecting the stroke so that the player gains a potential advantage for the stroke. Now, I’ll stress that this applies even when the action is accidental, as it was in Bryson’s case.”



When asked by reporters as he walked away whether he would return for Saturday’s third round, DeChambeau stopped short of giving any assurance. He instead headed to the practice range, where he began hitting balls as darkness fell over Royal Birkdale. DeChambeau’s agent Brett Falkoff said he would decide on Saturday morning whether he would continue playing but said his 32-year-old client is angry. “He’s a lot of things. He’s not a cheater,” Falkoff said. “He’s a big boy. He’ll see how he feels. But he certainly feels he was unfairly penalised.” DeChambeau is a popular player on tour but also divisive among fans, having defected to LIV Golf on a lucrative deal worth more than $100 million (USD).



Herbert was supposed to be paired with DeChambeau on Saturday but the latest drama means he will instead play his third round with Jackson Suber at 3.50pm local time (12.50am AEST). DeChambeau is listed to tee off at 3.30pm (12.30am) but if he pulled out of the tournament it would be unprecedented scenes. World.title: Ronnie Di Stasio on closing the pioneering Cafe Di Stasio after 38 years
World.content:
As the sun sets on one of Melbourne’s most influential Italian restaurants, its creator and his partner Mallory Wall remember the chaos, the hard times and St Kilda of old.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Restaurateur Rinaldo Di Stasio pulled an all-nighter on Tuesday as champagne-fuelled celebrations for the sale of Cafe Di Stasio morphed into a 5am World Cup watch party. His St Kilda hive of Italian good times this week passed into the hands of one of its former chefs, Nathan Presley, who will reopen it in August as a seafood restaurant. After 38 years, the Campari-soaked reign of 71-year-old Di Stasio over the Fitzroy Street dining room that helped propel Melbourne’s restaurant scene onto the global stage is over. 1 / 11 Regulars loved the restaurant's hedonistic atmosphere as much as its food.
